name: Romans

overview.author: The apostle Paul (1:1), written through his scribe Tertius (16:22).
overview.date: About AD 57, from Corinth near the end of Paul’s third missionary journey.
overview.audience: The church in Rome, made up of Jewish and Gentile believers, which Paul had not yet visited.
overview.setting: Paul planned to bring an offering to Jerusalem, then visit Rome on his way to Spain (15:22–29). Tensions existed between Jewish and Gentile Christians.
overview.purpose: To set out the gospel clearly: all have sinned, God justifies by faith in Christ, the Spirit gives new life, God is faithful to Israel, and the gospel transforms life and unites Jew and Gentile.
overview.structure: Introduction (1:1–17), the need for righteousness (1:18–3:20), justification by faith (3:21–5:21), new life in Christ and the Spirit (6–8), God’s faithfulness and Israel (9–11), the transformed life (12:1–15:13), and conclusion (15:14–16:27).

items.title: Gentiles, Jews, and all the world guilty
Peace with God; Adam and Christ
Freed from sin, the law, and condemnation
Sovereign mercy, Israel’s unbelief, and future hope

themes.title: The Gospel
themes.text: The power of God for salvation to everyone who believes (1:16).

themes.title: Universal Sin
themes.text: “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (3:23).

themes.title: Justification by Faith
themes.text: God declares sinners righteous through faith in Christ, apart from works.

themes.title: Union with Christ
themes.text: Believers died and rose with Christ and are no longer slaves to sin.

themes.title: Life in the Spirit
themes.text: The Spirit gives life, adoption, and help in weakness.

themes.title: God’s Sovereignty and Faithfulness
themes.text: God keeps His promises to Israel and shows mercy to all.

themes.title: Transformed Living
themes.text: Grace leads to renewed minds, sincere love, and unity.

christInBook.text: Jesus is descended from David and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection.
Christ is the propitiation for sin, showing God to be just and the justifier.
Christ, the second Adam, brings righteousness and life where Adam brought sin and death.
Christ died, was raised, and intercedes for us.
Confessing Jesus as Lord and believing God raised Him brings salvation.

crossReferences.note: Abraham believed and it was counted to him as righteousness.
The righteous shall live by faith.
Paul in Greece when Romans was written.

reflection: What would it look like to be “not ashamed of the gospel” this week?
How does Romans 5:8 change how you view God’s love when you fail?
Romans 6 says we are dead to sin. Where do you need to live out that freedom?
Which promise in Romans 8 do you most need today?
What does presenting your body as a living sacrifice (12:1) look like for you?

chapterList.title: The Gospel and Human Sin
chapterList.summary: Paul, a servant of Christ, greets the Roman believers and longs to visit them. “I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation.” God’s wrath is revealed against ungodliness. Though God is known through creation, people exchanged His glory for idols, so God gave them over to their desires.
questions: What is the gospel according to 1:1–4, 16–17?
How does creation reveal God (1:19–20)?
What happens when people exchange God’s truth for a lie (1:24–32)?

chapterList.title: God’s Impartial Judgment
chapterList.summary: Those who judge others while doing the same things condemn themselves. God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance. God judges impartially by works and the secrets of the heart. The Jews’ possession of the law doesn’t save them; true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit.
questions: How does judging others expose our own guilt (2:1)?
What is the purpose of God’s kindness (2:4)?
What does it mean to be a Jew inwardly (2:28–29)?

chapterList.title: Righteousness Through Faith
chapterList.summary: Jews have the advantage of God’s oracles, but all are under sin: “None is righteous, no, not one.” By works of the law no one is justified. But now God’s righteousness is revealed through faith in Jesus Christ. All have sinned and are justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiation.
questions: What does the list in 3:10–18 say about human nature?
What does “justified by his grace as a gift” mean?
How is God both just and the justifier (3:26)?

chapterList.title: Abraham’s Faith
chapterList.summary: Abraham was justified by faith, not works: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” David also speaks of the blessing of forgiveness. Abraham believed before circumcision, so he is father of all who believe. Hoping against hope, he trusted God to give life to the dead.
questions: Why is Abraham’s example so important to Paul’s argument?
How does 4:5 describe saving faith?
How did Abraham’s faith grow strong (4:18–21)?

chapterList.title: Peace with God
chapterList.summary: Justified by faith, we have peace with God and rejoice even in suffering, which produces endurance, character, and hope. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” As sin and death came through Adam, grace and life abound through Jesus Christ.
questions: What are the results of justification (5:1–5)?
How does suffering produce hope?
How are Adam and Christ compared (5:12–21)?

chapterList.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
chapterList.summary: Should we sin so grace may abound? By no means! In baptism we were united with Christ in death and resurrection. Consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God. Present yourselves to God. You were slaves of sin, now slaves of righteousness. “The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life.”
questions: Why doesn’t grace give us license to sin?
What does it mean to “consider yourselves dead to sin” (6:11)?
How does 6:23 summarize the gospel?

chapterList.title: The Struggle with Sin
chapterList.summary: Believers have died to the law and belong to Christ. The law is holy, but sin used it to produce death. Paul describes the struggle: “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me...? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!”
questions: What is the purpose of the law (7:7–12)?
How do you relate to the struggle in 7:15–24?
Where does Paul find deliverance (7:25)?

chapterList.title: Life in the Spirit
chapterList.summary: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” The Spirit gives life and adoption: we cry, “Abba! Father!” Present sufferings are not worth comparing with future glory. The Spirit helps us pray. All things work together for good. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ.
questions: What does “no condemnation” mean for your guilt?
How does the Spirit help us (8:14–16, 26–27)?
Which phrase in 8:31–39 encourages you most?

chapterList.title: God’s Sovereign Choice
chapterList.summary: Paul grieves over Israel’s unbelief. Not all descended from Israel belong to Israel; God’s promise works by His choice, as with Isaac and Jacob. God has mercy on whom He wills. The potter has rights over the clay. Gentiles have attained righteousness by faith, while Israel stumbled over the stone.
questions: How does Paul’s grief for Israel model love for the lost (9:1–3)?
How does 9:16 humble us?
What is the stumbling stone (9:32–33)?

chapterList.title: Confess and Believe
chapterList.summary: Paul’s prayer is for Israel’s salvation. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness. “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” Everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved. But how will they hear without a preacher? Faith comes from hearing.
questions: What is the gospel response in 10:9–10?
Why does Paul stress the need for preachers (10:14–15)?
How does faith come (10:17)?

chapterList.title: The Olive Tree and God’s Mercy
chapterList.summary: God has not rejected Israel; a remnant exists by grace. Israel’s stumbling brought salvation to the Gentiles, who are grafted into the olive tree. Gentiles must not be arrogant. A partial hardening has come until the full number of Gentiles comes in, “and in this way all Israel will be saved.” “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”
questions: What does the olive tree picture teach Gentile believers?
How does God use Israel’s stumbling for good?
Why does Paul break into praise in 11:33–36?

chapterList.title: Living Sacrifices
chapterList.summary: “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice.” Do not be conformed to this world but be transformed by renewing your mind. Use your gifts humbly in the body. Let love be genuine; rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, constant in prayer. Bless persecutors. Overcome evil with good.
questions: What does “living sacrifice” mean in daily life?
How is the mind renewed (12:2)?
Which command in 12:9–21 is hardest for you?

chapterList.title: Authorities and Love
chapterList.summary: Be subject to governing authorities, appointed by God. Pay taxes and honor. Owe no one anything except to love one another; love fulfills the law. The night is far gone; cast off the works of darkness and put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
questions: Why should Christians respect government?
How does love fulfill the law (13:8–10)?
What does “put on the Lord Jesus Christ” mean (13:14)?

chapterList.title: The Weak and the Strong
chapterList.summary: Welcome the one weak in faith without quarreling over opinions such as food and days. Each will give account to God. Do not judge or despise one another, and do not cause a brother to stumble. The kingdom is “righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.”
questions: What are “disputable matters” in today’s church?
Why should we not judge one another (14:10–12)?
How can you pursue what makes for peace (14:19)?

chapterList.title: Welcome One Another
chapterList.summary: The strong should bear with the weak and please their neighbor, as Christ did. Scripture gives endurance and encouragement. “Welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you.” Christ came so Gentiles would glorify God. “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing.” Paul shares his plans to visit Rome and Spain.
questions: How does Christ’s example shape our relationships (15:3, 7)?
What is the purpose of Scripture (15:4)?
Pray 15:13 for yourself and someone else.

chapterList.title: Greetings and Final Warnings
chapterList.summary: Paul commends Phoebe and greets many co-workers, including Prisca and Aquila, Andronicus, and Junia, many of them women. He warns against those who cause divisions. “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.” He closes with praise to the God who strengthens believers by the gospel.
questions: What do the many names reveal about the early church?
How should we respond to divisive people (16:17–18)?
How does 16:20 echo Genesis 3:15?

tagline: The gospel of God: righteousness by faith for Jew and Gentile
readingPlan: 16 chapters: one chapter a day takes 16 days; two a day takes about 8 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
